[[Category:Optimisation algorithm]]
[[Category:Artificial neural network]]

'''Gradient descent''' is an iterative [[optimisation algorithm]] used to find the local minimum of a differentiable function. 

It is the fundamental algorithm used to train many [[machine learning]] models, including [[artificial neural network (ANN)]].

== Mathematical definition ==

=== Goal ===

Let $f(\vec x)$ be a [[differentiable function]].

Gradient descent finds a value of $\vec x_n$ s.t $f_\text{min}=f(\vec x_n)$.

=== Process ===

Start with a reasonable guess $\vec x_0$ and iteratively updates according to the rule:

$$
\vec x_{t+1} = \vec x_t - \eta \nabla f(\vec x_t)
$$

until $\nabla f(\vec x_n) \to \vec 0$, then $\vec x=\vec x_n$ is a '''local minimum''' of $f$.

where:
*   $\vec x_t$ is the value of the $t^\text{th}$ iteration.
*   $\eta \in (0,1)$ is the '''learning rate'''
*   $\nabla f(\vec x_t)$ is the gradient of the function at $\vec x_t$.

<blockquote>
'''Why $-\nabla f$''': The gradient $\nabla f$ points in the direction of the steepest ascent. To minimise the function, move in the opposite direction for the steepest descent. 
</blockquote>

<blockquote>
Gradient descent is most useful for complex functions. For simple functions setting directly $\eta \nabla f(\vec x)=0$ and solve for $\vec x$ finds local extremum candidates. Evaluate $f$ at all candidate points and take the lowest value to obtain the global minimum of $f$, which is simpler and more accurate.
</blockquote>

== Mathematical example ==

{{Hidden example}}
Find $(x,y)$ that minimises

$$
f(x,y)=x^2+2y^2+3x-4y+6.
$$

around $(0,0)$.

'''Solution''':

$$
\nabla f(x,y)=
\begin{pmatrix}
2x+3\\
4y-4
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Using gradient descent with learning rate $\eta=0.1$ and initial point $(x_0,y_0)=(0,0)$,

$$
\begin{cases}
x_{t+1}=x_t-0.1(2x_t+3)=0.8x_t-0.3,\\
y_{t+1}=y_t-0.1(4y_t-4)=0.6y_t+0.4.
\end{cases}
$$

At $(x_0,y_0)=(0,0)$,

$$
\nabla f(0,0)=
\begin{pmatrix}
3\\
-4
\end{pmatrix},
$$

so

$$
(x_1,y_1)=(0,0)-0.1
\begin{pmatrix}
3\\
-4
\end{pmatrix}
=(-0.3,0.4).
$$

As observed, $(x_t,y_t)$ converges toward $(-1.5,1)$. Directly substituting the convergence values in, one finds $\nabla  f(-1.5,1)=\vec 0$. Hence $(-1.5,1)$ is indeed a local minimum around $(0,0)$.
{{End hidden}}

== Applications ==

=== Training [[artificial neural network (ANN)]] ===

Let $\mathbf{W}$ be the '''weight&biases matrix''' of an [[artificial neural network (ANN)]], $C(\mathbf{W})$ its '''cost function''', which measures the error between the model's predictions and the true values in the training set (e.g., [[sum of squared errors (SSE)]]).

Then '''training''' is iteration with step
$$
\mathbf{W}_{t+1} = \mathbf{W}_t - \eta \nabla C(\mathbf{W}_t).
$$
